transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-29 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~49 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Alex Rivera (CTO, Azimuth), Priya Nair (Infra), Samir Patel (Product)

Summary:
Brief intake to understand Azimuth's need for reserved GPU capacity, tenancy/isolation constraints, and burst/fallback strategy. High-level qualification: currently on hosted endpoints for experimentation, moving toward dedicated reserved nodes for production due to PII/regulatory constraints and cost predictability.

Topics: capacity reservation, isolation (tenant fencing/vpc), burst window handling, prewarm/hotpool strategies, KMS/HSM and SOC2 + SAML, benchmarking plan.

Transcript body (timestamps approximate, transcription imperfect):
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros, Liam's our solutions engineer. Alex, Priya, Samir, you good to go?
[00:08] Alex: Yeah yeah, thanks Maya. We're pretty tight on time, so we wanted to run through our capacity needs and sort out what dedicated looks like vs keepin' some workloads on hosted.
[00:15] Maya: Great. high-level: what are you running today? stack? models? latencies?
[00:22] Priya: Right now we're using a mix — small experiments on OpenAI hosted / endpoints for consumer-facing chat, and we have an internal on-prem cluster for sensitive inference. Production batch jobs run on our own infra but low QPS. We're evaluating Redwood Dedicated because we want reserved GPUs, isolation, and clear burst behavior.
[00:36] Liam: Cool. approximate qps and percent of traffic that needs private vs can be public?
[00:42] Samir: For initial rollout, it's 15-25 qps avg for our assistant use-case, peaks to ~120 qps during business-hours marketing spikes. Important: ~40% of that traffic touches PII / business-critical flows that have to stay inside VPC, the rest could go to hosted.
[01:02] Liam: And what model sizes / seq lengths are you planning? token sizes?
[01:06] Alex: We're primarily targeting a 13B open model for the assistant, sequence lengths around 1k tokens typical, but occasionally 2k+ for long context. We'll likely try quantized 8-bit and 4-bit for cost reasons, but we need to validate quality.
[01:20] Maya: Makes sense. so two asks: reserved capacity for the PII workload with isolation, and a burst/fallback plan to handle peak 120 qps. Any hard latency SLOs?
[01:31] Priya: p95 should be < 180ms for small requests, for longer context we can accept up to 500ms. Cold starts are a concern — we need consistent tail latencies.
[01:40] Liam: Ok noted. on prewarm/hotpool: we have options — warm pools (hotpool) with pre-warmed containers vs continuous reserved nodes. Prewarm reduces cold starts but costs more. Also automatic batching impacts latency; there's a tradeoff.
[01:56] Samir: We want predictable p95, so we probably need at least some dedicated warm capacity. But we also need burst headroom without committing for 100% peak.
[02:06] Maya: That's a common pattern — customers buy a baseline dedicated pool sized to handle 50-70% of expected peak and use burst on top with either reserved burst nodes or fall back to Redwood hosted with a policy that only spills non-PII traffic.
[02:21] Alex: Spill to hosted for non-sensitive traffic, yes. For sensitive flows, what's your approach for overflow? can we queue? degrade to smaller model?
[02:30] Liam: We can do multi-tier fallback: first try dedicated, then try smaller quantized variant on dedicated if available, then as a last resort drop to queued responses or degrade to a shorter context model. We can also route by policy so PII never leaves the VPC — that's preserved with private/redwood private path. But if you need absolute hard guarantees, dedicated + on-prem is the best.
[02:53] Priya: A few security Qs — do you support SSO/SAML? KMS integration? can HSM be used for key wrapping? audit logs?
[03:01] Maya: Yes to SSO/SAML and RBAC. For keys we integrate with KMS providers; HSM-backed KMS is supported in the private deployment. Audit logs are available with retention options. We'll share the SOC 2 and security pack.
[03:13] Alex: Great. also curious about network — VPC peering, egress rules, and data residency — can we keep everything within our AWS account?
[03:21] Liam: For Redwood Private we offer customer-managed VPC and peering; Dedicated can be run in a managed VPC with private networking. If you need the nodes inside your account (on-prem / air-gapped) that's the Private on-prem package. Otherwise we can provision dedicated nodes in a customer-isolated tenancy in our cloud region with VPC peering.
[03:39] Priya: How does tenancy/isolation work at the hypervisor level? do you do GPU multi-tenant on the same card or strict node-level tenancy?
[03:46] Liam: Reserved nodes are tenant-exclusive at the node level — no co-tenancy on the same GPU. There's also soft-fence options where multiple light tenants might share a node but we avoid that for strict isolation customers. We can map dedicated pools to host isolated jobs only.
[04:01] Alex: Ok good. what's the billing model for baseline + burst? hourly? monthly commit?
[04:06] Maya: Dedicated is typically a reserved commitment: monthly/annual commit per GPU-pool. Burst can be billed on-demand with higher unit cost or via a committed burst allowance. We can model a 6-month ramp and propose a blended rate.
[04:21] Samir: We also need to know about preemption risk and spot instances — we cannot use preemptible GPUs for PII traffic. Do you offer mixed strategies?
[04:30] Liam: Yes — spot/premarket only for non-sensitive workloads. For reserved pools we use non-preemptible hardware. We can also configure warm pools that sit idle but pre-warmed to reduce cold starts.
[04:42] Priya: What about autoscaling and burst automation — will it risk noisy neighbor impacting latency for the baseline tenants?
[04:50] Liam: Autoscaling respects the pool boundaries; burst nodes come from a separate pool. We also do smart routing that will avoid co-locating latency-sensitive tasks with heavy batch workloads. There's tracing and per-route dashboards in the console so you can see token-level latency and cost.
[05:06] Alex: Can we run our own quantization? like we have a custom quant pipeline, will Redwood accept customer-provided quantized model artifacts?
[05:13] Liam: We support common quant formats and can load quantized weights. There are constraints on supported kernel paths and we may need a short onboarding run to validate perf. Sometimes we see perf differences between 4-bit and 8-bit — we'll benchmark both.
[05:25] Maya: ok let's talk numbers for a moment — Priya, you said peak ~120 qps, average 15-25. how bursty is that? is it 2-3 short spikes or sustained?
[05:36] Priya: Usually sustained for 10-30 minutes during campaigns, sometimes sudden fanout for ten minutes. We also have sudden spikes from internal batch processes when a new model is deployed.
[05:45] Liam: For those shapes we recommend a baseline sized for the 75th percentile and a burst policy for 2x capacity for 30 minute windows. We'll simulate with the benchmark.
[05:55] Samir: We care about cost predictability — can you give an example of blended unit cost if we do 6k GPU hours reserved/month plus 2k burst hours?
[06:04] Maya: We'll send a pricing worksheet. quick sanity: reserved hours are discounted, burst billed at on-demand premium. We'll model that in the proposal.
[06:12] Alex: A couple of technical deep dive items — do you expose KV cache control? our app reuses long context K/V and we need to pin sessions to reduce recompute.
[06:22] Liam: Absolutely. We expose KV cache APIs, though the logger sometimes shows it as K-V cash in the UI (laughs) — transcription joke. But seriously, you can manage session affinity and cache TTLs. We also support prefix caching and shared cache strategies for templates.
[06:38] Priya: When you say prefix caching, you mean the runtime will reuse key/value pairs across similar requests? any consistency concerns if we update system prompts?
[06:46] Liam: Yes — updates to pinned prefixes invalidate caches; we support safe invalidation hooks. We'll show how to orchestrate rollouts without causing cache stampedes.
[06:55] Samir: On the compliance side, if we do Dedicated in your managed cloud, do you provide SOC2 + ISO attestation for the infra?
[07:03] Maya: We provide SOC 2 Type II for the platform and can share ISO docs. For Private on-prem deployments the attestation falls under your controls, and we assist with runbooks.
[07:12] Alex: Any constraints on model families? we want to test open weights (Open LLaMA style) and also maybe Mistral clones.
[07:19] Liam: We on-board a lot of open families; the main thing is verifying kernel compatibility and perf. We'll do a short model onboarding test during the benchmark.
[07:27] Priya: How about data retention and logs? we need logs to be ephemeral for PII flows and not retained beyond 30 days.
[07:33] Maya: We can configure log retention per route; for PII you can disable logs or route them through your KMS and lifecycle policy. We'll include options in the security questionnaire.
[07:44] Alex: Let's talk timeline — when can we start a pilot? we want to go live in production in ~9 weeks if everything checks out.
[07:51] Maya: That timeline is doable. pilot could be a 4-week dedicated trial with a reduced commit while we validate. After the benchmark and security review, we can spin up the baseline pool in ~2 weeks.
[08:00] Liam: For the benchmark we'll need your test harness, sample traffic, and the list of model variants. We'll run quantized vs non-quant, measure p50/p95/p99 and token cost.
[08:10] Priya: We'll need to make sure the benchmark includes our spike windows. I'll export the traces.
[08:15] Samir: Ok. around pricing — will you accept a 6-month ramp with commit adjustments?
[08:19] Maya: Yes — many customers do a ramp: smaller initial commit with committed bursts, then increase after pilot. We can do monthly billing with a true-up.
[08:27] Alex: Any gotchas we should watch for?
[08:29] Liam: Cold start behavior is the main thing — prewarm policies and warm pools mitigate it. Also ensure your batching configuration aligns with latency SLOs; aggressive batching can hurt p95. We'll recommend per-route batching thresholds.
[08:42] Priya: Regarding encryption at rest/in transit — we need FIPS-level TLS for some regulators. Do you support that in Private?
[08:49] Maya: Private/on-prem can be configured for FIPS/TLS profiles and HSM-backed KMS. We'll surface exact config options in the security pack.
[08:58] Alex: Great. let's recap next steps.
[09:01] Maya: Recap: we'll send the pricing worksheet + SOC2/security pack. Liam will prepare benchmark plan and propose dates. Priya will send spike telemetry. We'll set a benchmark week for early July. Anything else?
[09:13] Samir: Please include sample contract clauses for data residency and SLA with penalties for p95 breaches.
[09:19] Maya: Will do.
[09:21] Alex: Thanks everyone. We'll look for your email and the benchmark plan.
[09:26] Maya: Thanks — talk soon.

(Transcript notes: occasional mis-attribution and automated text errors e.g., "K-V cash" for KV cache, product names condensed, punctuation uneven.)
